p: child_process exposes four entry points with different trade-offs. spawn starts a program and gives you streams for its input and output, which is the choice for large or long-running output because nothing is buffered. exec runs a command through a shell and buffers the whole output into a callback, which is convenient for small commands and dangerous for anything that can produce megabytes. execFile skips the shell and runs one binary with an argument array, which is the safe form. fork is spawn specialised for another Node module and it opens an IPC channel for message passing.

The security rule is absolute: never build a command string from user input. exec, and spawn with shell: true, hand the string to a shell, so an argument containing a semicolon, a backtick or a dollar-parenthesis runs additional commands. Use execFile or spawn with an argument array, where the operating system passes each element as a distinct argument with no interpretation. On Windows the executable name must include the extension and shell built-ins such as dir are not executables at all, which is why cross-platform command execution needs a real path and, occasionally, an explicit shell chosen deliberately rather than by accident.

Exit codes and failure modes need explicit handling. A process that exits with a non-zero code emits 'exit' with the code, and a process that cannot be started at all emits 'error' instead of 'exit', so you must listen for both. When spawn is given an invalid command, the error arrives asynchronously and an unhandled 'error' event crashes the parent. Always attach the error handler before returning the child object, and treat a missing handler on the error event as a defect rather than a nuisance.

Capture output correctly by choosing streams over strings. The child's stdout and stderr are readable streams, so pipe them if you only want to pass them through, attach a data handler if you want to inspect them, and set a maximum accumulated size if you are collecting them. Ignoring stderr hides the most useful diagnostic information in the whole system. Setting stdio: 'inherit' wires the child directly to the parent's file descriptors, which is exactly right for a CLI that runs another tool and wants interactive output to behave.

Timeouts and cancellation are the caller's responsibility. There is no built-in timeout for spawn; use AbortSignal.timeout(ms) as the signal option, which kills the process and produces an AbortError, or set the timeout option on exec and execFile which sends a kill signal. Killing on POSIX sends SIGTERM by default, and a program that ignores SIGTERM will linger, so escalate to SIGKILL after a grace period. If the child spawns grandchildren, the signal reaches only the direct child unless you create a process group, which is a platform-specific detail worth isolating in one helper.

Environment variables are inherited by default and merged with the env option, not replaced. That means a child can see every secret in the parent's environment, so when you run a third-party tool, pass an explicit minimal env. Values must be strings; a number or undefined in the env object either throws or silently disappears depending on the platform, so stringify deliberately. The current working directory defaults to the parent's, and setting cwd is the reliable way to control where a tool resolves its own relative paths.

A Node process receives SIGINT when the terminal sends an interrupt and SIGTERM when a supervisor asks it to stop. Listen with process.on('SIGINT', handler). Installing a handler suppresses the default behaviour of terminating immediately, which is exactly the point: the handler can close servers, flush logs and finish in-flight work. SIGKILL cannot be caught and SIGSTOP cannot be caught, so they are the escalation path when a graceful stop does not complete.

A correct shutdown orchestrator has a single entry point and runs at most once. The first signal starts the sequence and flips a flag; any later signal is either ignored or, on the second one, escalated to an immediate exit. The sequence is: stop accepting new connections, wait for in-flight requests up to a deadline, close the database and other handles, flush logs, then exit with the appropriate code. Without the flag, a rapid double signal can start two overlapping shutdowns and produce confusing errors from a half-closed server.

Closing a server is not instantaneous. server.close stops listening and calls back once all existing connections have ended; with keep-alive connections that may be a long time, because an idle client holds the socket open. Node provides closeIdleConnections and closeAllConnections on the HTTP server to force the issue. The pragmatic pattern is to call close, wait a bounded interval, then call closeAllConnections and exit. Waiting forever is how a deploy hangs until the orchestrator escalates to SIGKILL and the process is killed mid-write.

Exit codes matter to whatever supervises you. Zero means success, a non-zero code means failure, and 128 plus the signal number reports death by signal in shell convention. process.exitCode is preferable to process.exit because it lets the event loop drain naturally; calling process.exit forcibly terminates pending asynchronous writes, which can truncate a log line or lose a database commit. Set the code, then let the loop empty. Reserve process.exit for the case where something is genuinely wedged and you have already tried to close cleanly.

The event loop and the process lifetime are linked. A Node process stays alive while there are pending timers, open sockets, active handles or refs. server.unref and timer.unref remove an object from the count so it no longer keeps the process alive, which is how you create a background timer that does not prevent exit. Conversely a forgotten setInterval keeps a process running forever and is one of the most common causes of a container that will not stop. Listing the handles with process._getActiveHandles in debugging shows what is holding a process open.

Uncaught errors are a last resort, not a control flow. An uncaught exception leaves the process in an undefined state, so the correct response is to log it in full, attempt a bounded cleanup and exit non-zero so the supervisor restarts you. An unhandled promise rejection terminates the process in current versions; treating that as a crash rather than ignoring it is the whole reason for the change. In both cases, install the handler at the very top of the entry point, before any other import can throw, so the handler exists for module-load failures too.

process.env is a plain object whose values are always strings or undefined. getenv with a default is a one-liner you should write once: const value = process.env.PORT ?? '3000'. Because the object is string-valued, a common bug is comparing process.env.DEBUG to a boolean or expecting process.env.TIMEOUT to be a number. Convert at the boundary and validate the result; a missing or malformed variable should be reported at startup with a clear message rather than producing NaN halfway through a request. Reading env once at startup into a typed configuration object makes the rest of the program free of string lookups.

stdio is configured per file descriptor as an array or a string shorthand. 'pipe' creates a stream, 'inherit' shares the parent's descriptor, 'ignore' discards it and a number shares an existing descriptor. Passing 'inherit' for all three is the same as stdio: 'inherit'. When you pass 'pipe' and then never attach a data handler, the child's write blocks once the pipe buffer fills, and the child hangs. That single mistake explains most cases of a child process mysteriously stalling forever while doing nothing observable.

Standard output is a stream with its own buffering, and it differs from standard error. When stdout is a terminal it is generally synchronous on POSIX, and when it is a pipe it is asynchronous. Writing a large amount of output and then exiting immediately can truncate the tail, because the process ends before the pipe drains. The reliable pattern for CLI tools is to await the drain of process.stdout.write, or to use process.exitCode and let the loop empty rather than calling process.exit. Standard error is unbuffered and is the right place for anything urgent.

Process metadata helps diagnostics and should be logged once at startup. process.pid identifies the process, process.ppid its parent, process.argv the arguments with the interpreter paths in the first two entries, process.execPath the interpreter's own path, process.platform and process.arch the target triple, and process.version the runtime version. process.argv0 is the original executable name. Logging the platform, architecture, runtime version and process id at boot turns a vague bug report into a reproducible one, and it costs a single line.

Working directory and paths are two different things. process.cwd returns the directory the process was started in and can change at runtime; __dirname and the module URL are fixed at load time. Both are absent in an ES module, where you derive them from import.meta.url instead: fileURLToPath(import.meta.url) gives the file path and dirname of that gives the module directory. Resolving a bundled asset relative to the current directory happens to work in development and breaks when a different directory launches the program, which is why asset paths should be derived from the module location or made absolute at startup.

Memory and load hints round out the picture. process.memoryUsage returns heapUsed, heapTotal, external and rss, and rss is the number an operator cares about because it includes the native allocations that a heap profiler does not show. process.resourceUsage gives CPU time and page faults. Tuning the heap with --max-old-space-size is the standard remedy for a container that the default heap limit makes look like it needs far more memory than it really does. None of these calls should appear in a hot request path; read them on a schedule and export them.

Node runs your JavaScript on a single thread, so any long synchronous computation blocks the event loop and stalls every other request. worker_threads runs JavaScript on additional threads inside the same process. Each Worker has its own V8 isolate, its own module registry and its own global object, so module-level state is not shared. A worker is started from a file path or an eval string with workerData passed to its constructor, and it signals completion with parentPort.postMessage. The main differences from a child process are cheaper startup and the ability to share memory.

Workers are the right answer for CPU-bound work: image processing, compression, parsing a large file, a cryptographic hash over many megabytes, or a pure algorithm that takes tens of milliseconds or more. They are the wrong answer for waiting on I/O, which should be asynchronous in the main thread anyway. A worker costs a few tens of milliseconds and several megabytes to start, so creating one per request is worse than the blocking it replaces. Create a pool once, keep the workers alive and queue tasks to them.

The thread boundary is a message boundary, so data is structured-cloned on the way across. Cloning is deep, handles circular references and preserves Dates, Maps, Sets, ArrayBuffers and BigInt, but it rejects functions, class prototypes and symbols — a plain object arrives as a plain object and loses its prototype. For large payloads the clone itself becomes the bottleneck, which is where transferable objects come in: passing an ArrayBuffer in the transfer list moves ownership rather than copying it, detaching it in the sender. Read the detached buffer and you get an empty one, which is the failure mode to expect when a transfer is accidentally reused.

SharedArrayBuffer allows genuinely shared memory between threads without cloning, combined with Atomics for lock-free coordination. Atomics.wait blocks the worker thread until a value changes and cannot be called on the main thread, which is deliberate — blocking the main thread is never the answer. Atomics.add and friends are the primitives for counters and simple locks. Use this only when the cloned copy is demonstrably the bottleneck; it is a real concurrency model with real data races, and most applications do not need it.

Lifecycle management is where worker code usually breaks. A worker emits 'online' when it starts, 'message' for messages, 'error' for an uncaught exception inside it and 'exit' with the exit code. An uncaught error in a worker does not crash the parent, so without an error handler a worker can die silently and its task hangs forever. Terminating is asynchronous and returns a promise; a worker running a tight loop that never yields will not terminate until it returns to the event loop unless you terminate with a forced option. Always pair a terminate with a timeout guard.

A minimal pool is a queue plus a fixed set of workers, each idle or busy, with the oldest queued task dispatched to the next worker that reports idle. Restart a worker on error rather than trying to reuse it, and cap the queue so memory does not grow without bound under load. A worker that throws on every task and is restarted on every task becomes an expensive crash loop, so count consecutive failures and degrade explicitly — reject the task, or fall back to running it on the main thread — instead of retrying forever.

The cluster module forks several processes that share one listening port. The primary process binds the socket and distributes incoming connections to the workers, so each worker handles a slice of the traffic with its own event loop and its own memory. On a machine with eight cores, running one process leaves seven idle; cluster or the equivalent built into a process manager is how you use them. Worker processes do not share memory, so any state such as a session cache or a rate-limit counter must move to a shared store.

The default distribution strategy differs by platform. On all platforms except Windows it is round-robin at the primary, which gives an even spread but can lead to a worker that is processing a slow request accepting new ones only in strict turn. The alternative is to let the operating system distribute the accepted connections, which smooths uneven request costs but can be unbalanced when connections are long-lived. Neither is universally better, and the choice matters more for keep-alive connections, where each connection sticks to one worker for its whole life.

Any in-memory state that assumed a single process must be revisited the moment you cluster. Idempotency keys, session data, rate-limit buckets, in-flight job registries, WebSocket connection lists and metrics counters are all per-worker unless externalised. This is the same set of concerns that appears when you add a second server, so treating them as shared from the beginning is the cheaper path. A worker count greater than the core count also hurts, because you are adding context switching and memory pressure without adding compute.

Graceful lifecycle in a cluster means the primary notifies the workers and they shut down in sequence, then the primary exits. If the primary dies without notice, the workers keep running as orphans; if a worker dies unexpectedly, the primary's 'exit' handler should decide whether to respawn. Assigning running tasks to worker ids, load balancing across heterogeneous machines or routes, and rolling restarts all become the primary's job. Beyond a handful of processes, a platform-level orchestrator is the better tool, and the in-process cluster module is really for making a single container use all of its cores.

Health and readiness are not the same check. A worker can be listening and still be unhealthy because its dependencies are down, or unhealthy because it holds stale configuration. A readiness endpoint that verifies the downstream dependencies and the loaded configuration lets the orchestrator remove an instance before it serves errors. Liveness should be a much shallower check, because a liveness probe that fails on a transient dependency outage will restart a perfectly good process and turn a degradation into an outage.

Memory is not shared, so the process count multiplies every per-process baseline. A 200 MB baseline across eight workers is 1.6 GB before any request is served. Workers also each load the runtime, the module graph and the JIT-compiled code. The practical implication is that clustering trades memory for throughput, and on a memory-constrained host it can be strictly worse than a single process. Measure the throughput and the resident set before and after, and be ready to run fewer workers with an explicit concurrency limit rather than assuming the core count is the right number.

A stream is a sequence of data delivered over time in four flavours: Readable, Writable, Duplex and Transform. Readable produces chunks, Writable consumes them, Duplex does both independently, and Transform is a Duplex whose output is derived from its input. Every stream carries chunks as strings or Buffers by default, and in object mode as arbitrary values. The whole point is bounded memory: a stream processes a gigabyte with a fixed buffer rather than loading the gigabyte into an array.

Streams have two modes and mixing them is a frequent source of lost data. Flowing mode pushes chunks to data handlers as fast as they arrive. Paused mode holds chunks until you call read. Attaching a 'data' listener switches a stream to flowing, and adding a 'readable' listener switches it back to paused; removing the last data listener does not automatically restore flowing mode. Piping and async iteration both manage this for you, which is why reading a whole file with chunks pushed through a data handler and separately awaiting a chunk in a loop can silently drop the chunks the other consumer took.

Backpressure is the property that makes streaming work. A Readable reports highWaterMark as the buffer size it is willing to have pending; read returns null when nothing is available; a Writable's write returns false when its internal buffer has exceeded its high water mark, and the caller is expected to stop writing until the 'drain' event. Ignoring a false return from write is the single most common stream bug, and it shows up as unbounded memory growth when the producer is faster than the disk or the network. pipe and pipeline honour backpressure automatically, which is most of the reason to use them.

Piping is convenient and error handling is its weakness. a.pipe(b) forwards data and ends b when a ends, but it does not propagate errors from a to b, and it does not destroy b when a errors. That gap is why pipeline exists: pipeline(a, b, c, callback) connects the streams, forwards errors in both directions and destroys every stream on failure, and in the promise form it rejects. Use pipeline, not pipe, for anything with more than one stage, and treat a bare pipe chain as a latent leak. Always give a pipeline an AbortSignal or a timeout when it reads from the network.

Choosing chunk sizes and encodings affects throughput measurably. A larger high water mark reduces the number of system calls and helps throughput on a fast local disk; on a network stream a large mark just increases latency and memory. Reading text streams with setEncoding('utf8') converts Buffers to strings and, importantly, handles characters split across chunk boundaries correctly. The same guarantee is not automatic if you decode each Buffer yourself. For compressed data a larger chunk size is generally better because the compressor has more context, so tune after measuring rather than assuming.

Object mode is a different beast with its own rules. In object mode a high water mark counts objects rather than bytes, and each chunk is an arbitrary value, so the throughput limit is often the per-object overhead rather than the payload. Object-mode streams are excellent for pipelines of transformation over records — parse a line, validate it, enrich it, write it — and terrible for large numbers of tiny values where the stream machinery costs more than the work. For millions of small records, batching into arrays and streaming the batches is usually the fastest correct design.

Every Readable is async iterable, so for await (const chunk of readable) is the cleanest way to consume one. It respects backpressure, it stops when the stream ends, and an error inside the loop propagates as a rejection. It does not automatically destroy the stream when you break out early, so when you stop before the end, call readable.destroy() in a finally block to release the underlying handle. The promise form of pipeline accepts an async iterable as a source, which makes the whole chain consistent.

Writable streams consume async iterables too via pipeline, and when you build a Transform you generally implement transform(chunk, encoding, callback) and push the result. The callback must be called exactly once, and calling it before push means the output has not been recorded yet, so the reader may see an empty result. In object mode, transform may push nothing to filter a record out, and may push several values to expand one input into many. Do not buffer the whole input to produce one output; that defeats the purpose of the stream and reintroduces the memory problem.

The modern constructor form is stream.Readable.from, Writable and Transform with objectMode options, rather than the function constructors of the early days. Readable.from accepts an iterable or async iterable and handles backpressure from a generator, which makes generators an excellent way to express a data source: a generator that yields chunks and pauses is pulled by the consumer, so a slow consumer slows the producer with no explicit queue. That pull model is the reason generators compose so well into pipelines.

Error handling must be explicit at every stage. A stream emits 'error' once and is then no longer usable; a second error is ignored. The pipeline form handles this, but a hand-written chain must attach an error listener to every stream, destroy the others, and avoid leaking the success callback. If a Writable errors after the reader has begun, the reader should see that error too, which is another thing pipeline does and pipe does not. An unhandled 'error' event on any stream is an uncaught exception and takes the process down.

Choosing to implement a custom stream is often unnecessary. Most transformations are better expressed as generator functions composed into Readable.from or as a Transform whose transform method is a few lines. Custom classes earn their place when you need control over the flush, the object mode boundary or the high water mark, or when you are wrapping a protocol such as a framer that must reassemble messages from arbitrary chunk boundaries. A line splitter is the canonical example: it must buffer a partial line until a newline arrives, and it must emit the trailing partial line on flush.

Finally, remember that not every file needs streaming. Reading a small configuration file or a single JSON document is simpler with readFile and JSON.parse, and the streaming version is roughly the same memory if the file is small but adds failure modes. The decision rule is the size relative to available memory and the latency you can tolerate. Streaming is for data that is large, unbounded, or arriving over time — logs, exports, uploads, network responses — and for everything else the direct read is clearer.

http.createServer takes a function that receives a request and a response and returns nothing; you write the response through the response object. The request exposes method, url, headers and the body as a readable stream. The response is a writable stream with setHeader, writeHead, write and end. Node's built-in server speaks HTTP/1.1 and supports HTTPS via https.createServer with a key and certificate, and HTTP/2 via the http2 module. For everything else you compose: framing, routing, body parsing, validation and error mapping are your responsibility.

The url on the request is the path and query only, never the full URL, and it is already percent-encoded. Parse it with new URL(req.url, 'http://' + (req.headers.host ?? 'localhost')) to get a URL object, then read pathname and searchParams. Reading req.headers is case-insensitive because the names are lowercased in the Node API, while the raw headers preserve the original casing and order in req.rawHeaders. Duplicate headers are joined with a comma in the standard way except for a short list including set-cookie, which is always an array.

The body is a stream, so reading it means either buffering it or streaming it. Buffering with for await (const chunk of req) gives you an array of chunks to concatenate, and you must bound the total size yourself: a request with no body limit is a trivially exploitable memory exhaustion, because an attacker can send an endless body. Set a maximum, count bytes as they arrive, destroy the request and answer with 413 when the limit is exceeded. Reading the body twice is impossible; if two middlewares both need it, one must buffer it once and give the parsed result to the other.

Response status, headers and body order are fixed: status and headers first, then the body. writeHead can only be called once and must come before the first write. Headers set after the response has started are silently ignored, which turns a late-set CORS or caching header into a subtle bug. For a JSON API, set content-type and content-length before writing, and end with the serialised body. Content-length is required for some HTTP/1.1 clients to avoid chunked framing, and omitting it means Node uses chunked transfer encoding, which is correct but precludes the client computing a progress percentage.

Keep-alive and timeouts control resource usage. The server keeps connections open by default, and the headers keepAliveTimeout and headersTimeout bound how long an idle connection or a slow header block may occupy a socket. The default headers timeout guards against a slowloris attack that opens many connections and sends headers a byte at a time. If you put a proxy in front, its timeouts must be longer than the application's, or the proxy will close connections the application considers healthy and produce sporadic 502s under load. Setting requestTimeout bounds the total time a request may take.

The server should handle the upgrade and clientError events rather than leaving the defaults. clientError fires when a client sends a malformed request; the default behaviour writes a 400 and the event is not fatal, but logging it reveals scanners and broken clients. The upgrade event is where a WebSocket implementation attaches, and if nothing handles it, Node destroys the socket. Both events are the seams where an observability hook belongs, and both are silent by default, which is why they are easy to omit and hard to debug later.

fetch is available in Node and follows the same rules as the browser version, with a few differences worth knowing. It rejects only on network failure, never on an HTTP error status, so res.ok must be checked explicitly. The response body is a stream that can only be read once; response.json() and response.text() both consume it, so clone the response before reading it twice. redirect is followed by default with 'follow', and setting it to 'manual' exposes the redirect response itself. The body can be a string, a Buffer, a stream or FormData, and setting the content-type header is your job for the first three.

Timeouts need to be explicit. There is no default timeout for fetch in Node, so a request to an unresponsive host can hang until the operating system's TCP timeout, which is measured in minutes. Pass an AbortSignal with AbortSignal.timeout(milliseconds) to bound the whole operation including the body read. For finer control, combine a connect timeout with a total timeout using AbortSignal.any, and remember that aborting after the response headers have arrived still aborts the body read. A request that is not bounded is a request that can consume a connection and a slot in your concurrency limit forever.

Retries are only safe for idempotent operations, and only for the failure classes that are actually transient. Retrying a connection refusal and a 503 with a delay is reasonable; retrying a 400, a 401 or a 422 is not, because the same request will fail identically. An explicit allow-list of retryable statuses and errors is safer than retrying everything that throws. Retrying a non-idempotent POST requires an idempotency key that the server understands, otherwise you will create duplicate resources, charge a card twice or send a message twice; there is no client-side fix for that.

Backoff should be exponential with jitter, and it must respect a maximum attempt count and a total deadline. Jitter — randomising the delay within a window — is what prevents a fleet of clients that failed together from retrying together and hammering the recovering service in synchronised waves. Honour the Retry-After header when it is present, because the server knows when it will be ready. Cap the delay so a user does not wait minutes for a page, and surface the failure rather than retrying silently beyond the point where a human is waiting.

Connection reuse is the throughput lever. A fresh TLS handshake per request costs multiple round trips, so keep an agent or an undici dispatcher with keep-alive enabled and a bounded pool size. In Node, undici is the HTTP client underneath fetch and exposes connection pooling, pipelining and per-origin limits through a dispatcher you can pass as the dispatcher option. Setting a sensible pool size and a keep-alive timeout aligned with the server's own timeout avoids a subtle failure where the client reuses a connection the server has just closed, producing an occasional spurious connection-reset error.

Reading a streaming response is where memory discipline matters again. A large JSON export can be tens of megabytes; consuming it with response.json() materialises the whole object, while iterating response.body as a byte stream lets you parse incrementally. For newline-delimited JSON, accumulate a buffer, split on newlines, parse complete lines and carry the remainder forward — the same boundary problem as any framing. When the consumer is slower than the producer, that natural backpressure from the reader propagates to the socket and keeps memory bounded without any explicit queue.

Structured logging means emitting objects, not sentences. A log line of { level, time, msg, requestId, userId, route, durationMs, status } can be filtered and aggregated; a sentence with the same information cannot. Write JSON to standard output, one object per line, and let the platform collect it. Keep levels small and meaningful — debug for development detail, info for state changes, warn for something recoverable, error for something a human should look at — and never log at info level in a loop that runs per item. The one field that pays for itself immediately is a request identifier generated at the edge and propagated to every downstream call.

Never log secrets, tokens, passwords, full credit card numbers or personal data, and do not rely on remembering that. Redaction belongs in the logger itself, applied by key name, so a developer who logs an entire request object by accident still gets the fields stripped. The most common leak is an error object that carries the request body or the headers in a property. Serialising errors requires care anyway: JSON.stringify of an Error yields an empty object because message and stack are not enumerable, so use a serializer that reads name, message, stack and cause explicitly.

Errors should carry context rather than being re-thrown bare. Wrap a low-level error in a domain error that names the operation, and attach the cause so the original stack is preserved; the cause property and the aggregate form are standard now. Answer with a stable machine-readable code and a correlation id, not a stack trace, and log the full detail server-side. An error handler that maps unknown errors to a 500 with a generic message and logs the real one prevents both information disclosure and vague bug reports.

Distinguish operational errors from programmer errors. A missing file, a validation failure and a downstream timeout are operational: handle them, convert them to a response, keep serving. A TypeError from a code path that should be unreachable is a programmer error: log it loudly and let the process crash so the supervisor restarts a clean instance, because continuing in an unknown state risks corrupting data. The visible symptom of getting this backwards is a process that limps along returning wrong answers, which is far worse than one that restarts.

Async context is where naive logging breaks down. A callback scheduled by a timer loses the request context unless you carry it explicitly. AsyncLocalStorage stores a value for the duration of an async operation and restores it across awaits, which is the mechanism that lets a logger attach the request id automatically without threading it through every function. Wrap the request handler in storage.run, store the context, and read it in the logger. The cost is small and the alternative is passing a context object through every layer of the application.

For the client side, capture errors at the top level and attach the build version and the route. A stack trace without the deployed commit is often useless because the source has moved on. Uploading source maps with the release, and resolving them on the server, converts minified frames into real ones. Rate-limit and deduplicate on the client so a render loop throwing every frame does not send thousands of identical events, and close the loop by linking each report to the request id if one exists.

Measure before optimising, and measure the thing that matters. For CPU, the inspector protocol exposes a profiler that records a sampling profile and aggregates it into a call tree with self and total time per frame. Node's --cpu-prof flag writes a profile on exit that the Chrome DevTools Performance panel can open. For the browser, the Performance panel records a trace with main-thread work, layout and paint. The first step in every case is the same: reproduce the slow path, capture a profile of it, and find the frame that owns the most time rather than the one that appears most often in the source.

Blocking the event loop is the most common performance defect in Node and the easiest to detect. The monitorEventLoopDelay histogram reports the delay between the loop's scheduled and actual wakeups, so a p99 delay of hundreds of milliseconds means something synchronous is hogging the thread. A synchronous JSON.parse of a huge payload, a regular expression with catastrophic backtracking, a synchronous file read and a big sort are the usual culprits. Instrument with per-phase timing, log anything above a threshold, and move genuinely CPU-bound work to a worker thread.

Memory leaks show up as a heap that grows across garbage collections and never returns to a baseline. Take a heap snapshot, exercise the suspected path, force a collection, take a second snapshot and compare the object counts by constructor. Common causes are a cache with no eviction, a listener added per request and never removed, a closure holding a large buffer alive through a small retained reference, and global arrays that accumulate history. Closures and listeners are the two that a leak detector identifies fastest because the retainer path points directly at the owning scope.

The distinction between a leak and a high-water allocation matters. An application that allocates a large buffer per request and releases it will show a sawtooth heap and a high resident set even though nothing leaks. A leak shows a monotonic floor that rises. Measuring the resident set alone conflates the two, so compare the heap used at the bottom of each sawtooth after an explicit collection. If the floor is flat, you have throughput pressure, not a leak, and the fix is pooling rather than hunting for a reference.

Flame graphs answer where the time goes for CPU-bound code and profiles answer where the allocations happen for memory-bound code. The two are complementary, and reading them is a skill: a wide frame high in the tree means many calls; a wide frame deep in the tree means an expensive leaf. Look for a leaf that dominates self time, then decide whether the fix is an algorithm change, fewer allocations or moving the work off the main thread. Micro-optimising a hot leaf that is called rarely, and therefore contributes nothing to total time, is the standard way to spend effort for no gain.

Load testing closes the loop but must be done carefully. Generating artificial load against a shared environment is disruptive, so test locally or in a dedicated environment, and ramp gradually. Watch the latency percentiles rather than the mean, because a mean hides the tail that users experience. Above saturation, throughput stops rising and latency climbs without bound; that knee is the useful capacity number. Pair the load test with an event loop delay histogram and a heap measurement to see which resource saturates first, because that is what to fix.

Debugging is remote inspection of a running process. Node accepts --inspect to open a debug port and --inspect-brk to stop at the first line, and a client such as Chrome DevTools or the editor's debugger attaches over the protocol. Attaching rather than adding log lines is faster for a control-flow question and, crucially, lets you inspect the live heap and the call stack at a breakpoint. In containers the debug port must be bound to a reachable address, and exposing it in production is a security risk because the protocol can execute code; keep it off by default and enable it deliberately for a session.

Source maps are what make a stack trace readable. Build with source maps enabled, ship them to the error tracker or keep them accessible to the server, and configure the runtime to use them. Node's --enable-source-maps makes stack traces resolve through the maps automatically, and the browsers do it natively. Without them a production stack trace points into minified code with names like t and e, and the cost of that in debugging time is much larger than the size of the maps.

Distributed tracing links a request across services. A trace has a global trace id and a parent span per operation, with timing, attributes and status; the trace id propagates in a header such as traceparent following the W3C Trace Context format. Instrumentation can be automatic for HTTP and database clients, or manual around a function that matters. Sampling is essential at volume: keep all errors, keep a small percentage of successes, and prefer tail-based sampling, which decides after the trace completes and therefore can keep the interesting ones. Correlating the trace id with the log line is what turns two tools into one investigation.

Health endpoints come in three kinds and conflating them causes outages. Liveness answers whether the process should be restarted and should be cheap and almost always true. Readiness answers whether traffic should be routed to it, and must check that dependencies are reachable and that configuration has loaded. A startup probe covers a slow first boot. Making liveness depend on a database turns a brief database blip into a fleet-wide restart storm, which is one of the most reliably self-inflicted outages in modern operations. Keep liveness shallow and let readiness carry the dependency checks.

Metrics should be chosen for the questions you will actually ask: request rate, error rate, duration percentiles and saturation of each constrained resource, broken down by the dimensions you use to decide, usually route and status class. Counter, gauge and histogram are the three types, and histograms are what make percentiles possible. Cardinality is the trap: labelling by user id or request id creates unbounded time series that will overwhelm the metrics backend. Stick to a small set of routes and statuses, and use exemplars or traces when you need to find one specific slow request.

The final discipline is to make debugging cheap before you need it. A single request id in every log line, every response and every trace; a version string in the health endpoint; a record of the deployed commit; timestamps in a consistent timezone; and an error tracker that groups by fingerprint. None of these are interesting features and all of them shorten an incident from hours to minutes. Building them is almost entirely mechanical, which is exactly why they get skipped under delivery pressure and exactly why they should be part of the first deploy rather than a follow-up.
